justification_text:
My probabilistic forecast presented a consistent point estimate of 621.52 across all time horizons: one day, one week, and one month. This identical value suggests an expectation of stability around a current or recently observed baseline. At the time of the forecast, the assessment indicated no strong, immediate drivers or trends anticipated to push the value significantly higher or lower in the short to medium term. This point estimate reflects a view that the value would likely persist around this level, implying a steady state or a reversion to a recent average in the absence of new, impactful information.

The widening of the 90% confidence intervals as the time horizon extends directly corresponds to the inherent increase in uncertainty over time. For the one-day forecast, the relatively narrow interval mainly captures typical day-to-day market fluctuations or minor data noise. However, as we look further out to one week and then to one month, the range of possible outcomes broadens considerably. This expansion is influenced by the increasing likelihood of various factors coming into play, such as new economic data releases, unexpected policy decisions, shifts in market sentiment, or even unforeseen geopolitical developments. These elements introduce greater variability and make precise predictions more challenging over longer durations.

While the provided intervals aim to capture 90% of the probable outcomes, certain high-impact or "black swan" events could push actual results beyond these bounds. Significant and sudden macroeconomic shifts, such as an unexpected spike in inflation, a rapid change in interest rates by central banks, or the onset of an unforeseen economic recession, could dramatically alter the value. Similarly, major geopolitical conflicts, sudden shifts in regulatory policy, or extreme supply and demand shocks specific to the forecasted item could lead to outcomes far outside the anticipated range. These types of rare, high-magnitude events are inherently difficult to predict and quantify within standard probabilistic models, representing the primary risks to the stated confidence intervals.
